tasks.title: What the script built
tasks.statement: The script is shell commands that build a network of namespaces, veth cables and bridges. Process the lines in order. Skip blank lines and lines starting with #; a line ending with a backslash continues on the next one (join them with a space). Drop a leading sudo. A command runs in the namespace host unless it is preceded by ip netns exec NAME or the flag ip -n NAME, in which case it runs in the namespace NAME. These commands are understood. ip netns add NAME creates a namespace with one interface, lo. ip link add NAME type veth peer name PEER creates both ends in the current namespace; ip link add NAME type TYPE without the word peer creates one interface (bridge, dummy and so on). ip link set [dev] NAME with one or more actions in a row: up, down; netns NS (moves the interface to another namespace; by the rule of this model a moved interface is down, with no addresses and no master); name NEW (a rename: ports attached to this interface as a bridge follow the new name); master BRIDGE (the bridge is in the same namespace). ip addr add CIDR dev NAME (or ip address add) appends CIDR to the end of the address list. Ignore everything else (ip route, ping, sysctl, ip -br addr and so on). Every new interface, lo included, is down, with no addresses and no master. The namespace host always exists and starts empty. The script is valid: everything it mentions already exists. Write a function netns_state(script): return a dictionary namespace → interface → {"up": bool, "addrs": [CIDR strings in the order added], "master": the bridge name or an empty string}.
tasks.hint: First join the lines with a trailing backslash, then split each into tokens: drop sudo, work out the namespace, then look at t[0] and t[1]. In link set walk the remaining words in a loop: netns, name and master take two words each.

tasks.title: Will the ping cross the bridge
tasks.statement: A model of a network on one host. state is a dictionary namespace → interface → {"up": bool, "addrs": [CIDR], "master": a bridge name or ""}; pairs is a list of veth end pairs written as ["ns/interface", "ns/interface"]. The model has no routes and no forwarding: a packet travels only at layer 2. Write a function can_ping(state, pairs, src_ns, dst_ip): return True if a ping to dst_ip from the namespace src_ns succeeds, otherwise False. Rules. An interface with a non-empty master is a bridge port: its addresses are ignored and it neither sends nor receives packets itself. If dst_ip belongs to an up interface (not a port) of src_ns itself, the answer is True. Otherwise the source is an up interface S of src_ns (not a port) with an address A whose network contains dst_ip (the connected route). A frame from S reaches the other end of its veth pair: both ends of the pair must be up. If the partner end Q is a port of a bridge M, the frame enters the bridge: M must be up, and then the addresses of the bridge M itself are reachable, as are the partner ends of other ports of M for which both the port and its partner are up. If Q is not a port, only Q itself is reachable. If S is itself a bridge (it has ports), the reachable ends are the partner ends of its up ports whose partner is up; S itself must also be up. The target is found when a reachable up non-port interface E has an address exactly equal to dst_ip and also an address whose network contains the source address A (the reply has to get back). If no pair S and E is found, return False.
tasks.hint: Build a dictionary of partners from pairs. Write a helper far_ends(ns, name) that returns the list of reachable "ns/name" strings; then loop over sources and their addresses and compare the ends' addresses with ipaddress.ip_interface.

tasks.title: Which step is missing
tasks.statement: A ping from a namespace to the outside world fails. You get command outputs. addr_out is ip -br addr inside the namespace (columns: name, state, addresses; the name may look like eth0@if12); route_out is ip route inside the namespace; forward_out is the single line of sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward on the host, for example net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0; nat_out is iptables -t nat -S POSTROUTING on the host; gateway is the bridge address that must be the gateway; uplink is the name of the host's outgoing interface. Check in order and return the code of the first cause found. link-down: there is no interface (other than lo) whose state is exactly UP. no-address: the UP interfaces have no IPv4 address; the namespace address is the first token of the form a.b.c.d/n on the first such interface. no-default-route: route_out has no line whose first word is default. wrong-gateway: the first such line does not contain via and the gateway address. ip-forward-off: the value after the = sign (stripped) is not 1. no-masquerade: there is no suitable rule. A suitable rule starts with -A, has -j MASQUERADE or -j SNAT, and its conditions do not exclude the namespace: if there is -s NET (without a ! before it), NET must contain the namespace address; if there is -o NAME, NAME must be uplink; if there is ! -o NAME, NAME must not be uplink. A rule with no conditions fits. If a suitable rule exists, return ok.
tasks.hint: Go through the checks top to bottom as listed. For rules split the line on spaces: the token after -s is the network, and the token before -o tells whether it is negated.

tasks.title: Ports after masquerade
tasks.statement: Several namespaces go out through one host, and masquerade replaces the source address with host_ip. Two different outgoing connections cannot have the same set (protocol, source address and port after translation, destination address and port), or the kernel could not tell their replies apart. The model: connections arrive in order and stay open. flows is a list of [proto, src_ip, sport, dst_ip, dport] (sport from 1024 to 65535). Write a function masquerade(host_ip, flows): for each connection return the string host_ip:port. Port choice: if the tuple (proto, port, dst_ip, dport) is not yet taken, the port stays as it was (sport). Otherwise take the first free port counting up from sport + 1; after 65535 counting continues from 1024. A connection with the same full original set (proto, src_ip, sport, dst_ip, dport) as one already seen is the same table entry: it gets the same answer and takes nothing. This is a simplified model: the real kernel searches for a free port differently, but the uniqueness principle is the same.
tasks.hint: Keep a set of taken (proto, port, dst_ip, dport) and a dictionary of original sets already seen. The search for a free port is a loop that wraps 65535 → 1024.

tasks.title: Where a packet to a published port goes
tasks.statement: rules is the text of iptables-save for the nat table (the lines *nat, :CHAIN, -A CHAIN conditions -j TARGET, COMMIT and comments; only the -A lines matter). A packet enters the PREROUTING chain and goes through the rules top to bottom. A rule fires if all its conditions hold; these are understood: -i NAME and ! -i NAME (the incoming interface in_iface), -p PROTO and ! -p PROTO, --dport N or N:M (an inclusive range; with ! it is negated), -d ADDRESS[/MASK] and ! -d (the destination address dst_ip), -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL (true if dst_ip is in local_ips). Ignore the other words (-m tcp, -m udp and so on). Skip a rule without -j. Targets: DNAT with --to-destination ADDRESS[:PORT] means a translation is found and the walk ends; if there is no port, dport stays. ACCEPT ends the walk without a translation. RETURN leaves the current chain for the calling one (from PREROUTING it ends without a translation). The name of a chain that exists in rules is a jump into it; when it ends or returns, the rules of the calling chain continue after the jump. Any other target (LOG, MASQUERADE and so on) does nothing. Write a function dnat_dest(rules, proto, dst_ip, dport, in_iface, local_ips): return the string "address:port" of the new destination, or an empty string if the packet is not translated.
tasks.hint: Collect the rules per chain into a dictionary. A recursive function walk(chain) returns dnat, accept or return; after a jump into a user chain, continue only if it returned return.

tasks.title: What conntrack shows
tasks.statement: The output of conntrack -L (or the file /proc/net/nf_conntrack): one connection per line, the first word is the protocol (tcp, udp, icmp). If a line starts with the words ipv4 or ipv6 and a number, skip them: the protocol is the next word. The line has two sets of fields: the first (after the first src=) describes the client's packet, the second (after the second src=) says how the reply will arrive. A set has src, dst and, for tcp and udp, sport and dport. The other words (the state, [ASSURED], [UNREPLIED], packets=, bytes=, mark=, use=, type=, code=, id=) are not needed. Skip lines that lack two sets (blank lines, the closing line conntrack ... flow entries have been shown). Write a function nat_entries(text): for each suitable line return a tuple (proto, kind, client_seen_as, server_real). kind: snat if the reply set's dst differs from the original src or (when ports exist) the reply dport differs from the original sport; dnat if the reply src differs from the original dst or the reply sport differs from the original dport; both if both hold; none if neither. client_seen_as is dst:dport of the reply set (how the external server sees the client), server_real is src:sport of the reply set (who really answers). For lines without ports (icmp) both values are just an address.
tasks.hint: Split the line into words and walk them: a word starting with src= opens a new set; put dst, sport and dport into the last open set (the first occurrence of each key).

tasks.title: Where the packet was lost
tasks.statement: An administrator started a ping to an external address from a namespace and at the same time captured tcpdump -n at several points of the path: points is a list of [point_name, output_text] ordered from the namespace outward. The text has tcpdump's service lines and packet lines like 10:15:01.123456 IP 10.200.0.2 > 203.0.113.9: ICMP echo request, id 4242, seq 1, length 64 (a link-level header from the -e flag may precede IP). An echo request is a line with ICMP echo request where the address after > equals remote; a reply is a line with ICMP echo reply where the address before > equals remote; consider only lines whose id equals icmp_id (do not compare the request's source address: masquerade may have replaced it). Write a function locate_drop(points, remote, icmp_id): return one of these strings. no-request: the request is not seen at the first point (or there are no points). request-lost-after:NAME: the request is seen at the first k points in a row but not at point k+1 (NAME is the name of the last point where it is seen; go by the first gap). If the request is seen at every point: no-reply, if the reply is not seen at the last point; reply-lost-after:NAME, if the reply is seen at the last point but, moving from the last point toward the first, it vanishes: NAME is the last point on that way where the reply is still seen (the first gap going backwards); ok, if the reply is seen everywhere.
tasks.hint: The regular expression IP (\S+) > (\S+): ICMP echo (request|reply), id (\d+), parses a line; for each point compute two flags, request seen and reply seen, then apply the rules in order.

tasks.title: Whose end of the cable is it
tasks.statement: An administrator looks at the list of interfaces on the host and wants to know in which namespace (container) the other end of each veth lies. You get host_links, the output of ip -o link on the host, and ns_links, a dictionary namespace name → the output of ip -o link inside it. A line starts with the index and the name: 25: veth3a2b1c0@if24: <BROADCAST,...; the name may look like NAME@ifN (N is the partner's index in another namespace), or NAME@partner_name (the partner is in the same namespace), or just NAME. The same index numbers are not unique across namespaces, so check the pair from both sides. Write a function veth_owners(host_links, ns_links): for every host interface of the form NAME@ifN return, in a dictionary, NAME → "namespace/interface", where the interface inside the namespace has its own index N and its name carries @ifM with M equal to the host interface's index. If there is none in any namespace, the value is an empty string. If several fit, take the first namespace alphabetically. Do not include in the answer host interfaces without @ifN (lo, eth0, bridges, a partner in the same namespace).
tasks.hint: The regular expression ^(\d+):\s+([^:@\s]+)(?:@(\S+?))?: extracts the index, the name and the optional partner from each line. For a host interface go through the namespaces alphabetically.

tasks.title: Subnets from pools, Docker style
tasks.statement: A container network manager gives every new network a subnet from address pools. pools is a list of [base, size] in priority order, for example ["172.17.0.0/16", 16] or ["192.168.0.0/16", 20]: subnets with the prefix length size are cut from the base. used is a list of CIDRs already taken on the host (routes, existing networks); they can be of any size and need not lie on pool boundaries. Write a function allocate_subnets(pools, used, count): return a list of count new subnets (CIDR strings) in the order of issue. The model: pools are scanned in order; inside a pool the candidates go in ascending address order; a candidate is taken if it overlaps no used subnet and none already issued in this call. Skip a pool whose size is smaller than the base prefix length or larger than the address's maximum length. If candidates run out earlier, return as many as were found. For count of zero or less return an empty list. This is a model: the real Docker daemon does something similar, but the details depend on the version.
tasks.hint: ipaddress.ip_network(base).subnets(new_prefix=size) yields candidates in ascending order; the overlap test is cand.overlaps(t). Add issued subnets to the list of taken ones too.
